analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for companies to hide serious product dangers from regulators and workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or any cosponsors in the House; it died in committee when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it a federal crime for a company, or a manager responsible for a product, to knowingly hide a serious danger that ordinary use of a product could kill or seriously injure someone. Companies and managers would have had 15 days to warn a federal agency and their own workers in writing, or immediately if the risk was imminent. Hiding the danger could mean a fine or up to five years in prison. Firing or punishing an employee for sounding the alarm would also have been a crime, punishable by a fine or up to a year in prison, and a manager's fine could not be paid by the company on their behalf.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who handle dangerous products and would have been warned in writing rather than kept in the dark. Consumers, because companies would have had to report hidden dangers to regulators quickly. Whistleblowers, who would have gained criminal-law protection against being fired or punished for reporting a serious danger.

how_it_helps.text: A company or product supervisor who knows of a serious danger—a hidden risk that normal use of a product could cause death or serious injury—would have to tell a federal agency in writing and warn affected employees in writing within 15 days, or immediately if the risk of death or serious injury was imminent. Knowing failure to do so would carry a fine, up to five years in prison, or both.

Retaliating against an employee—through firing, demotion, or discriminatory treatment—because that person warned coworkers or told a federal agency about a serious danger would itself be a crime, punishable by a fine, up to one year in prison, or both.
If a manager is fined, the company could not pay that fine for them, directly or indirectly, so the penalty would land on the person who made the decision to stay silent.
The bill explicitly would not preempt state law, so states could keep or add their own protections on top of it.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that make or sell products in interstate commerce, and the managers responsible for production, quality control, research, or regulatory filings, who would face criminal liability if they sat on a known serious danger. Compliance costs—documenting, notifying agencies, and warning workers—would fall on those businesses, and could be passed to consumers in prices.

drawbacks.text: The criminal standard would reach a broad set of managers—anyone whose duties 'may fairly be assumed to represent the policy' of the company, including people in quality assurance, research, or agency filings—so a fifteen-day reporting clock backed by five years of prison exposure could push companies toward over-reporting or defensive lawyering rather than faster honest disclosure.

The definition of a 'serious danger' covers any reasonably foreseeable use that could cause death or serious injury, including harm from repetitive motion or disease, which is a wide net for a criminal statute and could create uncertainty about when the reporting duty is triggered.

Criminal penalties can be a blunt tool; an honest supporter would acknowledge that civil and regulatory penalties often reach conduct faster than prosecutions, and that prosecutors would bear the burden of proving what a company 'knew' and when.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: workers and the public would learn about hidden dangers much sooner, and whistleblowers would get real protection, in exchange for new criminal exposure and compliance costs for product makers. The bill's biggest design weakness is breadth—vague definitions and a five-year prison term for a manager who misses a deadline create room for both overreach and evasion. A narrower, better-drafted version could deliver most of the safety benefit with less ambiguity, but the idea itself is a direct answer to a real gap: today, concealing a known product danger from workers and regulators is generally not a federal crime.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the 115th Congress, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then sent to its crime subcommittee three weeks later, and nothing further ever happened; no one else signed on and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the Dangerous Products Warning Act on January 3, 2017, the opening day of the 115th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced.
On January 23, 2017, it was referred to the subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations; no hearing, markup, or floor action followed.
The bill drew no cosponsors during its two years in Congress.
The bill would have amended the federal criminal code to penalize concealing serious product dangers and retaliating against employees who report them.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies and product managers that might have faced criminal liability for concealing serious dangers, and for retaliating against warning employees, are better off because the bill never advanced. Workers and consumers never got the warning and anti-retaliation protections it would have created.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no Republican signed on, so the partisan shape can only be read from sponsorship: a single Democrat introduced the bill and it drew zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.industry: Product manufacturers and sellers (consumer goods, industrial products, and services in interstate commerce)
industries.note: The bill would have created federal criminal liability—fines and up to five years in prison for managers—for knowingly concealing a serious product danger, plus liability for retaliating against employees who speak up. Its interest ran against the public here: the value of staying silent about a known danger is avoiding recalls, liability, and lost sales, which is exactly what the bill targeted.

industries.industry: Corporate officers and compliance, quality-control, and R&D managers
industries.note: The bill defined 'product supervisor' broadly, reaching managers in quality assurance, research, and regulatory filings, and barred companies from paying their fines. Honest managers who disclosed promptly faced no penalty, but those who miscalculated the deadline faced prison exposure.
